entry: [[Australia|Australian]] external territory in the [[Indian Ocean]] (pop., 2021: 1,692), about 350 km south of [[Java]] and [[Sumatra]]. The island covers 135 sq km, and most residents live in settlements on its northern edge. [[Phosphate|Phosphate deposits]], originally formed as [[Guano|guano]], led Britain to annex the island in 1888, and commercial mining began in 1899. Japan invaded in 1942, and the territory was transferred to Australia in 1958. Christmas Island National Park covers 63% of the island, and the island's isolation has produced a high level of endemism among its flora and fauna.

Song or hymn on the theme of [[Christmas]], traditionally sung at Christmas itself or during the surrounding holiday season. The term noel has sometimes been used for carols, especially those of French origin. The first known Christmas hymns date from 4th-century Rome, when Latin hymns such as *Veni redemptor gentium* by [[Ambrose]] stated the doctrine of the Incarnation in opposition to [[Arianism]]. By the 13th century, popular carols in vernacular languages had developed in France, Germany, and Italy, particularly under the influence of [[Francis of Assisi]]. Carols were originally communal festival songs and were adopted for church use later. [[Martin Luther]] promoted congregational singing after the Protestant Reformation, and carols were sung privately during the Puritan ban on Christmas in England. The 19th-century revival included "God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen" and "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing," which appear in William Sandys' 1833 collection.

Austrian, German, and American actor. Waltz had a substantial career in German television and theater before his international breakthrough. He won two [[Academy Awards]] for Best Supporting Actor, for playing Hans Landa in [[Quentin Tarantino]]'s *Inglourious Basterds* (2009) and for Dr. King Schultz in *Django Unchained* (2012). He also played Ernst Stavro Blofeld in the [[James Bond]] films *Spectre* (2015) and *No Time to Die* (2021).

British and American author and journalist. Born and educated in Britain, Hitchens graduated from the [[University of Oxford]] in 1970 and moved to the United States in the early 1980s to write for *The Nation* and *Vanity Fair*. Originally a [[Socialism|democratic socialist]], he was one of the "Four Horsemen" of New Atheism alongside [[Richard Dawkins]]. He supported the [[Kosovo War]] and [[Bosnian War]], and after 9/11 he argued for the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan. His politics were widely viewed as drifting to the right, though he called himself a "leftist."

American actor and film producer. Lambert was raised in [[Geneva]] and later in [[Paris]], and he became internationally famous for playing Tarzan in *Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes* (1984). He won a César Award for Best Actor for *Subway* (1985). He is best known for playing Connor MacLeod in *Highlander* (1986) and in the franchise that followed. He also played Raiden in *Mortal Kombat* (1995) and served as executive producer of *Nine Months* (1995).

English actor and singer. Lee's career spanned over 60 years, and he often played villains in horror and franchise films. He played [[Count Dracula]] in seven Hammer Horror films, beginning with *Dracula* (1958). He played Francisco Scaramanga in the [[James Bond]] film *The Man with the Golden Gun* (1974), then Saruman in the *The Lord of the Rings* film trilogy (2001–2003) and Count Dooku in *Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones* (2002). He was knighted in 2009 for services to drama and charity.

English playwright, poet, and translator of the Elizabethan era. Marlowe was the first to achieve critical reputation for his use of blank verse, which became the standard for the era's drama, and his plays, including the two parts of *Tamburlaine*, *Doctor Faustus*, and *Edward II*, are distinguished by overreaching protagonists. Scholars consider him the foremost dramatist in London in the years before his death, and some believe he greatly influenced [[William Shakespeare]]. He studied at Corpus Christi College, [[Cambridge]], where in 1587 the university hesitated to award his degree over a rumor that he intended to become a Catholic priest; the Privy Council intervened, praising his "faithful dealing." Accounts of his death are contested by scholars. An official coroner's account, discovered only in 1925, describes a fatal stabbing in a Deptford rooming house during an argument, but scholars dispute the full story.

British and American filmmaker. Nolan is known for complex storytelling in Hollywood blockbusters, and he is considered a leading filmmaker of the 21st century. His feature debut was *Following* (1998), and *Memento* (2000) brought him international recognition. His films include *The Dark Knight* trilogy (2005–2012), *Inception* (2010), *Interstellar* (2014), and *Dunkirk* (2017). *Oppenheimer* (2023) won [[Academy Awards]] for Best Director and Best Picture. Two of his films are among the highest-grossing of all time, and his works often explore memory and personal identity. He was knighted in 2024 for his contributions to film.

Canadian actor. Plummer's career spanned seven decades in film, stage, and television. He became a household name as Captain Georg von Trapp in *The Sound of Music* (1965). He was the only Canadian recipient of the "Triple Crown of Acting," with an Academy Award, two Tony Awards, and two Primetime Emmy Awards. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *Beginners* (2011) and was nominated for playing [[Leo Tolstoy]] in *The Last Station* (2009). He also received Tony nominations for [[Othello]] and [[King Lear]].

American actor, activist, director, and author. Reeve played the title role in the *Superman* film series (1978–1987) and later directed *In the Gloaming* (1997). In 1995 he was paralyzed from the neck down after being thrown from a horse in Culpeper, Virginia, and he used a wheelchair and ventilator for the rest of his life. He then lobbied for spinal injury research, including human embryonic [[Stem cell|stem cell]] research, and for better insurance coverage for people with disabilities. He led the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation and died of [[Cardiac arrest|cardiac arrest]] at a hospital near his home in Westchester County, New York.

American actor. Walken won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for playing a troubled [[Vietnam War]] veteran in *The Deer Hunter* (1978). He was nominated for the same award for *Catch Me If You Can* (2002). His films have grossed more than $1.6 billion in the United States. He has hosted [[Saturday Night Live]] seven times, and he has played the lead in Shakespeare plays including [[Hamlet]] and [[Macbeth]].

English architect, astronomer, mathematician, and physicist. He is one of the most highly acclaimed architects in English history, known for work in the English Baroque style. After the [[Great Fire of London]] in 1666, Wren was responsible for rebuilding 52 churches in the City of London, including his masterpiece, St Paul's Cathedral. Although the creative responsibility for several of these churches is now more commonly attributed to others in his office, notably Nicholas Hawksmoor, Wren also designed the Royal Hospital Chelsea and the south front of Hampton Court Palace. Educated in Latin and Aristotelian physics at the [[University of Oxford]], he was a founder of the Royal Society and served as its president from 1680 to 1682. His scientific work was highly regarded by [[Isaac Newton]] and [[Blaise Pascal]].

Set of [[Laboratory|laboratory]] techniques for separating [[Mixture|mixtures]] into their components. A mixture is dissolved in a fluid mobile phase, which carries it through a column, plate, or sheet coated with a stationary phase. Its constituents separate because they have different affinities for the stationary phase and travel at different apparent velocities. Botanist Mikhail Tsvet developed the method in the early 1900s to separate plant pigments such as [[Chlorophyll]], which form colored bands, and he coined the term. Preparative chromatography purifies components for later use at higher cost, while analytical chromatography uses smaller amounts of material to identify analytes or measure their proportions. Archer John Porter Martin and Richard Laurence Millington Synge won the 1952 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for partition chromatography, which encouraged paper, gas, and high-performance liquid chromatography.

Chemical element with [[Atomic number|atomic number]] 24 and symbol Cr. It is a steel-gray, lustrous, hard, and brittle [[Transition metal|transition metal]] in group 6 of the periodic table, valued for its high [[Corrosion|corrosion]] resistance and hardness. [[Stainless steel]] and chrome plating together account for 85% of commercial use, and polished chromium reflects almost 70% of visible light. Louis Nicolas Vauquelin discovered the element in 1797. The name comes from the Greek *chrōma*, meaning color, because many chromium compounds are intensely colored. Industrial production begins with chromite ore (mostly FeCr₂O₄), which is converted to ferrochromium for producing alloys such as stainless steel. Trivalent chromium occurs naturally in foods and is sold as a [[Dietary supplement|dietary supplement]], although evidence of nutritional benefit is insufficient. Hexavalent chromium, or chromate, is toxic and [[Carcinogen|carcinogenic]].

Package of [[DNA]] containing part or all of the genetic material of an organism. In eukaryotic cells, the DNA is coated with histones, proteins that condense it and maintain its integrity, and the chromosome has a complex three-dimensional structure that plays a role in transcriptional regulation. Chromosomes are visible under a light [[Microscope|microscope]] mainly during metaphase of cell division, when they are highly condensed and each consists of two sister chromatids joined by a centromere. Recombination during [[Meiosis]] contributes to genetic diversity. Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, and extra copies of a chromosome, or aneuploidy, can cause conditions such as [[Down syndrome]]. The word comes from Greek *khrôma* ("color") and *sôma* ("body"), describing the strong staining produced by dyes.

Long-term [[Lung|lung]] disease involving poor airflow, comprising chronic [[Bronchitis|bronchitis]] and [[Emphysema|emphysema]]. It progressively makes breathing harder and cannot be cured, but treatment and lifestyle changes can control symptoms and slow progression. The strongest risk factors are [[Tobacco smoking|tobacco smoke]], [[Air pollution|air pollution]], and workplace dust and chemical fumes, and genetics can also play a role. Symptoms include progressive shortness of breath, persistent cough, and wheezing. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by lung function tests, and treatments include inhaled medications, pulmonary rehabilitation, and oxygen therapy for advanced disease. As of 2021, the disease affected about 213 million people worldwide and was the fourth-biggest cause of death, responsible for approximately 5% of total deaths.

Neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated trauma to the head. Its symptoms include behavioral, mood, and thinking problems, and it often worsens into [[Dementia|dementia]]. Most documented cases occur in athletes in [[Boxing]], [[Mixed martial arts]], and contact sports such as [[American football]]. Risk is driven by the cumulative number of repetitive head impacts, not by diagnosed concussions. Diagnosis is possible only at [[Autopsy|autopsy]], and there is no specific treatment. The largest study found CTE in 6% of the general population.

Science of arranging events in their order of occurrence, such as in a timeline. It is part of periodization and of history, including Earth history and the study of the [[Geologic time scale|geologic time scale]]. Chronology relies mostly on chronometry and [[Historiography|historiography]]. Relative chronology places events in sequence, while absolute chronology assigns calendar dates. [[Radiocarbon dating]] estimates the age of formerly living things by measuring the proportion of carbon-14 in their carbon, and dendrochronology dates wood by matching tree rings to regional reference sequences. The Christian era, founded by Dionysius Exiguus about 500 and extended by [[Bede]], is now the most widespread dating system on Earth, while an epoch is the date, usually a year, when an era begins.

History and projected future of the universe according to [[Physical cosmology|physical cosmology]]. The earliest stage supported by observational evidence is [[Cosmic inflation|inflation]], which occurred 13.8 billion years ago and expanded space extremely rapidly. Its energy became particles and radiation, initiating the [[Big Bang]]. Within the first three minutes, nucleosynthesis formed [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]], [[Helium|helium]], and a small amount of [[Lithium|lithium]]. About 380,000 years later, electrons combined with nuclei to form stable [[Atom|atoms]], making the universe transparent to photons and producing the [[Cosmic microwave background]]. Gravity then formed the first stars and galaxies. After a further nine billion years, dark energy came to dominate and accelerate expansion. Many modifications to the standard timeline have been proposed, but direct observational evidence is lacking for its earliest phases.

Genus of perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the [[Asteraceae|daisy family]]. Native to East Asia and northeastern Europe, with its center of diversity in [[China]], the genus blooms in autumn and is associated with November in the Northern Hemisphere. Chrysanthemums were first cultivated in China as early as the 15th century BCE, and more than 500 [[Cultivar|cultivars]] had been recorded by 1630. By 2014, more than 20,000 cultivars were estimated to exist worldwide. Cultivation in Japan began in the Nara and Heian periods and flourished in the [[Edo period]], when many flower shapes were developed. The imperial crest of Japan is a chrysanthemum, and the monarchy is also called the Chrysanthemum Throne. The name derives from the Greek *chrysos* ("gold") and *anthemon* ("flower").

American automaker and subsidiary of Stellantis, headquartered in Auburn Hills, Michigan. Founded in 1925 by Walter Chrysler from the remains of the Maxwell Motor Company, it is one of the "Big Three" U.S. automakers. It sells vehicles under the Chrysler, Dodge, Jeep, and Ram nameplates. After a 2009 bankruptcy reorganization supported by the U.S. government, Fiat acquired the company in 2014. It became part of Stellantis in 2021 through the merger of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles and PSA Group.

American guitarist, singer, and songwriter and a pioneer of [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]]. Nicknamed the "Father of Rock and Roll," Berry refined [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]] into the major elements that made rock and roll distinctive. His hits included "Maybellene" (1955), "Roll Over Beethoven" (1956), and "[[Johnny B. Goode]]" (1958), whose lyrics focused on teenage life and consumerism and whose style featured guitar solos and showmanship. Berry was among the first inductees into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1986, and "Johnny B. Goode" is the only rock-and-roll song on the [[Voyager Golden Record]]. He was imprisoned in 1962 under the Mann Act for transporting a 14-year-old girl across state lines.

American television producer, writer, director, and composer. Nicknamed the "King of Sitcoms," Lorre created or co-created sitcoms including *Cybill* (1995–1998), *Dharma & Greg* (1997–2002), *Two and a Half Men* (2003–2015), *The Big Bang Theory* (2007–2019), and *Mom* (2013–2021). He was also an executive producer of *Roseanne*. Lorre won two Golden Globe Awards for his work on *Roseanne* and *Cybill*.

American martial artist, actor, screenwriter, and author. He held black belts in [[Karate|karate]], [[Taekwondo|taekwondo]], Tang Soo Do, [[Brazilian jiu-jitsu]], and [[Judo|judo]], and he founded his own discipline, Chun Kuk Do. After playing a villain opposite [[Bruce Lee]] in *The Way of the Dragon* (1972), he became an action star with *Good Guys Wear Black* (1978). Cannon Films signed him as its leading star in the 1980s, and in the 1990s he played the title role in the [[CBS]] series *Walker, Texas Ranger* (1993–2001). In 2005 he became the subject of "Chuck Norris facts," an [[Internet meme|internet meme]].

Easternmost federal subject of Russia, in the Russian Far East. Anadyr is the capital and largest town. The okrug has been the only autonomous okrug not subordinate to another federal subject since it separated from Magadan Oblast in 1992. It is the seventh-largest federal subject and the least densely populated in Russia. The closest point between Russia and the United States measures 88.51 km, and the okrug shares a maritime border on the [[Bering Strait]] with [[Alaska]]. The economy depends on gold, coal, and other mining, along with fishing and reindeer herding.
